edition.deck: A reported cyber incident has disrupted the UK’s benefits systems; fresh accounts detail threats to companies supplying Ukraine, while Denmark and the wider world face a crowded evening agenda.

content.headline: Houthi attacks put Saudi Arabia’s image of security to the test
content.shortHeadline: Houthi attacks test Saudi Arabia’s image of security
content.standfirst: Missile and drone strikes have repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia since an informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled. Riyadh’s busy streets suggest daily life continues, but residents and businesses are living with alerts, disruption and the risk of further attacks.

image.caption: A Houthi attack targeted an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October.

sources.originalTitle: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security

segments.body: Saudi Arabia is facing a sharp rise in Houthi attacks, including a strike on Riyadh’s airport on 10 October that killed 13 people and injured more than 300, according to the BBC’s reporting. An analysis of conflict data recorded 274 attacks between 1 July and 25 November; most were intercepted, but at least 41 were not.

segments.title: Security and daily life
segments.body: The attacks have hit prominent buildings and disrupted flights, challenging Saudi Arabia’s effort to present itself as a safe place for residents, visitors and investors. Restaurants and shops in Riyadh remain busy, but residents describe phone alerts and the sound of air defences as reminders that not every incoming strike is stopped.

segments.title: Wider consequences
segments.body: The renewed fighting has also brought worsening conditions in Yemen. The BBC reports that more than 360,000 people have been displaced since August, while over 800,000 people in areas around Taiz are cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to Unicef. Saudi-led air strikes and Houthi attacks add to risks for civilians.

content.headline: Ukraine says children from occupied areas were sent to a North Korean camp
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says children from occupied areas were sent to North Korea
content.standfirst: Reports that children from Russian-occupied Ukraine attended a camp in North Korea have triggered a diplomatic dispute: Pyongyang has ordered a Swiss diplomat to leave after Switzerland joined EU sanctions linked to the camp.

image.caption: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un at the Songdowon children’s camp in 2014.

sources.originalTitle: En børnelejr i Nordkorea har udløst et diplomatisk opgør med Schweiz

segments.body: North Korea has given Switzerland’s diplomat in Pyongyang 48 hours to leave and ordered the closure of the Swiss diplomatic office, which had reopened less than a month earlier. The dispute follows Switzerland’s decision to join EU sanctions targeting, among other things, an international children’s camp in Wonsan.

segments.title: Allegations about the camp
segments.body: Ukrainian children, including children from Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, are alleged to have attended the camp. A Ukrainian public broadcaster previously identified a 12-year-old boy from occupied Makiivka who went there in 2025. Information from inside North Korea is limited; a Danish defence-college lecturer says the reported programme appears intended to indoctrinate children.

segments.title: A diplomatic rupture
segments.body: North Korea has condemned the sanctions as hostile and a violation of its sovereignty but has not directly addressed the allegations about Ukrainian children. Switzerland says diplomatic relations are not being severed; contacts are to continue through its embassy in Beijing and North Korea’s embassy in Bern. Experts cited by DR link Pyongyang’s response to its closer relationship with Russia.

content.headline: Canada’s top court upholds most of Quebec’s religious-symbols ban
content.shortHeadline: Canada’s top court upholds most of Quebec’s religious-symbols ban
content.standfirst: The Supreme Court of Canada has largely upheld Quebec’s Bill 21, which bars some public-sector workers from wearing religious symbols. It also ruled that elected officials cannot be barred from wearing religious face coverings under the law.

sources.originalTitle: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants

segments.body: Canada’s Supreme Court has confirmed the validity of most of Quebec’s 2019 law banning public-sector workers in certain roles from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and cross. The law was enacted using the constitution’s notwithstanding clause, which allows governments to override some rights protections.

segments.title: A limit on the law
segments.body: The court ruled that Quebec’s elected officials cannot be barred from wearing religious face coverings. It also said courts can declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even when the notwithstanding clause is invoked, though it did not make such a declaration in this case.

segments.title: Rights in dispute
segments.body: Civil-liberties groups have argued Bill 21 disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab and excludes them from parts of public life. Three of the seven justices dissented on parts of the ruling, saying the law infringes on freedom of religion, freedom of expression and equality rights.

content.headline: Spain’s final election debate centres on housing and a possible far-right role
content.shortHeadline: Spain’s election campaign ends with housing and Vox in focus
content.standfirst: Voters go to the polls on Sunday as polls point to a possible government led by the conservative People’s Party with far-right Vox support. The final debate put housing affordability at the centre of a campaign also shaped by the cost of living and immigration.

image.caption: Protesters in Spain have used jangling keys as a symbol of frustration over housing costs.

sources.originalTitle: Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in

segments.body: Spain’s main party leaders made their final televised appeal to voters before Sunday’s election, with housing dominating the debate. Polls suggest the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may not secure another term, while the conservative People’s Party is projected to finish first and could govern with support from Vox.

segments.title: Housing and the vote
segments.body: The parties offered sharply different remedies for the housing crisis. The People’s Party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, promised to build one million homes; Vox leader Santiago Abascal said his party would prioritise Spaniards for housing aid; and left-wing candidates argued for stronger tenant protections and action against landlords. Sánchez defended measures including rent caps.

segments.title: A wider test
segments.body: The BBC’s reporting from Valencia describes renters unable to plan for the future as prices rise faster than their incomes. The vote also tests whether Vox could enter national government for the first time since Spain’s return to democracy; immigration and the cost of living have been other major campaign issues.

content.headline: Kenyan court convicts cult leader over 123 more deaths
content.shortHeadline: Kenyan cult leader convicted over 123 more deaths
content.standfirst: Paul Mackenzie was convicted of manslaughter after a court found he directed adult followers to fast to death in Shakahola forest. The verdict follows his 200-year prison sentence earlier this month for the murder of 191 people, mostly children.

image.caption: Paul Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves.

sources.originalTitle: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths

segments.body: A court in Mombasa has convicted Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie of the manslaughter of 123 adult followers, whom it found he had directed to fast to death in Shakahola forest between 2021 and 2023. Twenty-nine other defendants, including Mackenzie’s wife, were also convicted; 60 were acquitted.

segments.title: Earlier convictions and appeal
segments.body: Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass-killing case. He had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter; one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing. Prosecutors have indicated they will appeal the acquittals.

segments.title: The wider questions
segments.body: The court said Mackenzie systematically persuaded followers to fast until they died, with children, women and then men expected to die before him. The deaths have intensified scrutiny of oversight of religious activity in Kenya. A commission of inquiry established by President William Ruto was later declared unconstitutional.

content.headline: Former Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years for pregnant student’s murder
content.shortHeadline: Former Kenyan governor jailed for pregnant student’s murder
content.standfirst: Zacharia Okoth Obado, two former aides and a county clerk were sentenced over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno. Both Obado’s and Otieno’s legal teams say they plan to appeal.

image.caption: Zacharia Okoth Obado was sentenced over the 2018 murder of Sharon Belyne Otieno.

sources.originalTitle: Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years over pregnant girlfriend's murder

segments.body: Former Migori County governor Zacharia Okoth Obado has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for the murder of Sharon Belyne Otieno, a university student who was seven months pregnant. Two former aides were also sentenced: Michael Oyamo received 25 years and Caspal Ojwang’ Obiero 18 years.

segments.title: The court’s findings
segments.body: The court found that Obado provided the motive and financial resources, Oyamo coordinated the killing and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime. Otieno was abducted after leaving a hotel with journalist Barrack Oduor, whom she had contacted to discuss her relationship with Obado. Oduor escaped and his account became an important lead.

segments.title: Appeals planned
segments.body: Obado and Otieno’s legal teams say they will appeal. The judge rejected a request for the death penalty and declined to award compensation to Otieno’s family, saying there was not enough evidence to establish the claimed financial losses.

content.headline: Kyiv faces another winter of strikes, blackouts and uncertainty
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine braces for a winter of strikes and blackouts
content.standfirst: A BBC report from Kyiv describes daily alerts, damaged infrastructure and residents preparing for another winter under bombardment. The correspondent also finds that many Ukrainians remain determined to resist, despite exhaustion and doubts about a peace deal.

sources.originalTitle: John Simpson: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in

segments.body: Kyiv is entering winter with power cuts, water shortages and frequent air-raid alerts after Russian attacks on electricity infrastructure and bridges. BBC correspondent John Simpson reports that some residents have left the city and some businesses have closed as strikes and disruption make daily life increasingly difficult.

segments.title: Resilience under strain
segments.body: The report describes people sheltering during attacks and struggling through darkened streets and high-rise blocks without reliable power or water. A Ukrainian poll cited by Simpson found 62% of respondents were prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, while 79% believed Ukraine would ultimately win; these are survey findings, not a guarantee of public opinion everywhere.

segments.title: No clear path to peace
segments.body: Simpson argues that the war’s underlying aims make a negotiated settlement difficult: he writes that Ukrainians he spoke to distrust Russia’s willingness to honour an agreement, while the reported US proposals have not addressed questions such as reparations or how to prevent another invasion. Russia denies targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure.

content.headline: Italy’s former police chief denied Mafia inquiry claims in letter before death
content.shortHeadline: Former Italian police chief denied Mafia inquiry claims in letter
content.standfirst: Gianni De Gennaro’s eight-page letter rejects allegations that he misled an inquiry into the 1992 killing of anti-Mafia judge Paolo Borsellino. Investigators are examining digital material said to contain notes from his career.

image.caption: Gianni De Gennaro became Italy’s police chief after working in the anti-Mafia directorate.

sources.originalTitle: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death

segments.body: Former Italian police chief Gianni De Gennaro denied obstructing the investigation into the 1992 killing of anti-Mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in an eight-page letter written shortly before his death. His body was found at his home in Tuscany on Saturday; authorities believe he took his own life, and a post-mortem examination was due on Friday.

segments.title: An unresolved investigation
segments.body: De Gennaro, who worked in Italy’s anti-Mafia directorate before becoming police chief, was accused in a recent inquiry of misdirecting the initial investigation. He denied the allegation in the letter, which was published by Corriere della Sera. The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino’s killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone.

segments.title: Digital evidence under review
segments.body: Investigators have seized hard drives and USB sticks reportedly labelled “Stato-Mafia” and “Massacres”. Forensic specialists are expected to examine whether files were altered or deleted. The allegations and De Gennaro’s death have revived public attention to the unresolved questions surrounding the Mafia killings of the early 1990s.

content.headline: DWP cyber incident takes most pensions and benefits services offline
content.shortHeadline: DWP cyber incident takes most benefits systems offline
content.standfirst: The Department for Work and Pensions says regular payments will continue, but many online services have been unavailable since Thursday. The cause is not yet known, and officials say there is no current evidence of customer data loss.

image.caption: The DWP is working with the National Cyber Security Centre after taking services offline.

sources.originalTitle: DWP ‘cyber incident’ knocks almost all pensions and benefits systems offline

segments.body: Most UK pensions and benefits systems were unavailable on Friday after the Department for Work and Pensions took services offline as a precaution following unusual activity. People could not use affected services to check a state pension, claim Universal Credit or apply for disability benefits.

segments.title: Payments and investigation
segments.body: The DWP says regular pension and benefit payments are not affected and will be made as normal. Some members of the public reported missing expected payments, while one Universal Credit claimant told the BBC she was worried about bills due before the payment she was told would arrive by Monday.

segments.title: Cause still unknown
segments.body: The department is working with the National Cyber Security Centre and says there is currently no evidence of customer data loss or that a malicious actor targeted other government departments. The investigation is ongoing; officials have not established publicly whether the incident was a cyberattack.

content.headline: UK defence firms supplying Ukraine prepare for threats of sabotage and espionage
content.shortHeadline: UK defence firms supplying Ukraine prepare for sabotage threats
content.standfirst: A rare MI5 and Ministry of Defence warning has led companies to review security, according to employees and industry sources. The reporting describes suspected Russian-linked activity across Europe, while one expert cautions that the campaign is intended to disrupt support for Ukraine rather than signal an imminent war with Europe.

image.caption: A photo illustration accompanying reporting on security threats to UK defence suppliers.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Beware of attractive women’: Russian honeytrap warning for UK defence workers
‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank

segments.body: UK companies involved in supplying weapons to Ukraine have been warned by MI5 and the Ministry of Defence about risks including sabotage, arson and intimidation. The i Paper reports that a Midlands drone manufacturer has told staff to watch for surveillance, treat external emails cautiously and be alert to attempts to extract information.

segments.title: A wider pattern
segments.body: The report describes suspected attacks and plots involving defence companies in several European countries, including arson, surveillance and threats to executives. Data from threat-intelligence firm Dragonfly, cited by The i Paper, counted 42 confirmed or suspected Russian sabotage incidents involving European defence sites or people from June to mid-November, compared with 12 in the first five months of the year.

segments.title: Risk and intent
segments.body: The International Institute for Strategic Studies says Russian-linked sabotage has increased and warns that a mass-casualty incident is possible, though it does not establish that one is imminent. Dragonfly’s Matthew Ince says the activity is aimed at disrupting the flow of defence equipment to Ukraine, not necessarily preparing for conflict with Europe. Moscow rejects accusations that it is behind the campaign.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s account adds first-hand detail from a UK drone manufacturer: staff have been advised to watch for suspicious vehicles and phishing, while firms are considering measures including bodyguards and counter-drone protection.

content.headline: Former Labour adviser arrested again in China espionage investigation
content.shortHeadline: Former Labour adviser arrested in China spy investigation
content.standfirst: Matthew Aplin has been arrested on suspicion of an offence under the Official Secrets Act, in a continuing investigation into alleged Chinese interference. Police have not publicly specified what conduct is alleged, and Aplin was released under investigation.

image.caption: Matthew Aplin, a former Labour communications officer in Wales, has been arrested in the investigation.

sources.originalTitle: Ex-Labour adviser arrested for ‘breaching Official Secrets Act’ in China spy probe

segments.body: Matthew Aplin, a former Labour Party communications officer in Wales, has been arrested on suspicion of an offence under the Official Secrets Act 1911. He was one of three men initially arrested in March as part of an investigation into suspected assistance to a foreign intelligence service.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: The Metropolitan Police said all three men were interviewed under caution again in late November. Two were released on bail until December; Aplin was released under investigation. Police have not publicly set out what he is alleged to have done under the Official Secrets Act, and inquiries continue.

segments.title: Political context
segments.body: The UK government says the broader case concerns suspected foreign interference targeting British democracy. Security minister Dan Jarvis says Chinese officials have been formally challenged in London and Beijing. Aplin’s former employer confirmed he had been suspended from his role at a Cardiff public-affairs agency.

content.headline: Poundland enters administration, putting jobs and suppliers at risk
content.shortHeadline: Poundland enters administration as jobs and suppliers face uncertainty
content.standfirst: The discount chain’s 600 UK and Irish stores remain open while administrators consider bids. More than 10,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers face uncertainty, with some suppliers saying they are owed substantial sums.

image.caption: Poundland stores remain open while administrators consider bids for the chain.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Punched in the guts’: Poundland staff left reeling as it goes into administration

segments.body: Poundland has entered administration after its US-based owner, Gordon Brothers, rejected at least two solvent offers and declined further funding. All of its approximately 600 UK and Irish stores remain open while administrators consider bids, but staff and suppliers face an uncertain future ahead of Christmas.

segments.title: Workers and creditors
segments.body: More than 10,000 employees are at risk if stores close or the chain is broken up. Suppliers say they are owed money for goods already delivered, and some have stopped sending stock. One independent confectionery supplier told the Guardian it was owed £68,515; another reported a debt of more than $1.2m.

segments.title: What happens next
segments.body: Potential buyers have been given until Sunday to submit bids. Gordon Brothers says it provided £85m in new finance and that efforts to preserve jobs and stores will continue under the administrators. Workers quoted in the report say they are worried about closures and the difficulty of finding replacement jobs.

content.headline: Only a third of rough sleepers offered support under Christmas pledge
content.shortHeadline: A third of rough sleepers offered support under Christmas pledge
content.standfirst: At least 3,276 people sleeping rough in England were offered a bed or support in October, compared with an estimated 9,369 sleeping rough in September. The figures do not show how many accepted an offer or moved off the streets.

image.caption: Shelter says rough sleeping remains shockingly high across England.

sources.originalTitle: A third of rough sleepers offered bed or support after Burnham Christmas vow

segments.body: Government figures show at least 3,276 people sleeping rough were offered a route off the streets in October under Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Christmas pledge. That is just over a third of the estimated 9,369 people sleeping rough in England in September, the latest month with a national estimate.

segments.title: What the figures do not show
segments.body: The data does not say how many offers were accepted or resulted in people moving off the streets. Big Issue founder John Bird said the government should publish that information, warning that refusing unsuitable accommodation should not be treated as a success. The government says outreach teams will continue to work with people who do not accept an initial offer.

segments.title: Uneven progress
segments.body: The proportion offered support varied across England, and many councils could not provide complete data. About 63% of councils said they were confident of offering everyone a route off the streets by 1 December. Shelter said offers must lead to a permanent home and support, not only a bed in a hostel.

content.headline: Government backs bill to curb lawsuits used to silence journalists
content.shortHeadline: Government backs bill against lawsuits used to silence critics
content.standfirst: Labour will support a cross-party bill intended to let courts dismiss abusive lawsuits against journalists, whistleblowers and others at an early stage. Campaigners warn the proposed test may be too difficult and costly for defendants to use.

sources.originalTitle: Labour backs bill to stop lawsuits used to silence journalists and whistleblowers

segments.body: The government has said it will support a private member’s bill intended to prevent wealthy or powerful claimants using strategic lawsuits against public participation, known as Slapps, to silence critics. The bill is sponsored by Conservative MP John Whittingdale and seeks to let courts dismiss abusive cases before defendants incur unaffordable legal costs.

segments.title: Concerns about the test
segments.body: The UK Anti-Slapp Coalition says the proposed early-dismissal process is too complicated, sets too high a bar and could leave defendants facing financial risk. Campaigners say proving a claimant’s intention to cause harm may require a costly mini-trial. The government believes the current draft balances protection from abuse with access to the courts.

segments.title: A bill, not yet a law
segments.body: The bill has a better chance of passing with government support, but its passage is not guaranteed. Existing protections apply only in cases involving alleged economic crime; the proposed legislation would cover a wider range of public-interest reporting, including sexual abuse and corruption.

content.headline: England expands pharmacy flu vaccinations for children as admissions rise
content.shortHeadline: Pharmacies offer children flu jabs as hospital admissions rise
content.standfirst: More than 6,000 pharmacies in England are being asked to vaccinate children who missed school jabs, as flu admissions climb earlier than in recent years. Appointments are due to open through the NHS from Monday.

image.caption: Pharmacies in England are offering nasal-spray flu vaccinations to children aged two and three.

sources.originalTitle: Parents urged to vaccinate children for flu as hospital cases surge in England

segments.body: Parents in England are being urged to arrange flu vaccinations for children who missed school-based jabs. For the first time, more than 6,000 high-street pharmacies are being asked to offer appointments, with bookings due to open on Monday and vaccinations from Tuesday.

segments.title: Admissions rising early
segments.body: The UK Health Security Agency reported nine flu admissions per 100,000 people in England last week, up from five the week before and 4.9 in the equivalent week last year. It said emergency-department attendances for flu-like illness were above seasonally expected levels. A programme lead said the rise was arriving weeks earlier than last season.

segments.title: Why vaccinate children
segments.body: Health officials say vaccinating children can protect them and reduce the chance of infection spreading to younger siblings and older relatives. More than 3.5 million children from reception to Year 11 have already been vaccinated. Pharmacies are also offering nasal-spray vaccinations for two- and three-year-olds.

content.headline: Manchester’s £4bn Victoria North project faces questions over delays
content.shortHeadline: Manchester’s £4bn Victoria North project faces scrutiny over delays
content.standfirst: Residents say promised replacement homes have been delayed, while the city council and developer point to more than 1,000 completed homes and construction-sector obstacles. The reporting also examines the project’s finances and disputes over the development partnership.

sources.originalTitle: Inside Burnham’s £4bn Manchester new town… a ghost estate of boarded-up streets

segments.body: Manchester’s Victoria North regeneration project promises 15,000 homes across seven neighbourhoods, but residents in Collyhurst say they have waited years for replacement council homes and that boarded-up streets have become a feature of the area. One resident who expected to move in 2021 says the latest estimated date is spring 2027.

segments.title: Progress disputed
segments.body: The i Paper reports that more than 1,000 homes have been completed in the wider scheme, while only 10 social-rent homes in Collyhurst are complete. The developer says more than 1,000 homes are under construction or completed; Manchester City Council says 1,196 have been delivered and 1,104 are on site, while acknowledging progress in Collyhurst has been slower than expected.

segments.title: Financial and legal questions
segments.body: The report examines the joint venture’s losses and liabilities, delays in construction and a dispute involving a rival developer over land within the project area. The council and developer say the scheme has faced rising costs and other industry challenges; the figures and disputes described are not, by themselves, evidence of wrongdoing.

content.headline: Data breach exposes 15,338 students’ phone numbers and SMS details
content.shortHeadline: Data breach exposes 15,338 students’ phone numbers and SMS details
content.standfirst: A breach at SMS provider OnlineCity.io exposed phone numbers and message details linked to students at 23 Danish upper-secondary schools. Authorities warn other organisations using the provider’s services may also be affected.

image.caption: The breach exposed student information held by a supplier used by 23 upper-secondary schools.

source.credit: Foto: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Over 15.000 gymnasieelevers telefonnumre lækket
Tusindvis af gymnasieelevers telefonnumre er blevet lækket
Styrelse følger sikkerhedsbrud hos teleudbyder - flere organisationer ventes ramt

segments.body: A security breach at OnlineCity.io/GatewayAPI exposed 15,338 phone numbers belonging to students at 23 Danish upper-secondary schools, according to Gymnasiefællesskabet. Unauthorised users had access to server log files from 22 October to 22 November, the organisation says.

segments.title: More than phone numbers
segments.body: The breach was wider than first reported: users also accessed sender IDs and the first 20 characters of SMS messages, including some sent through the Secret Class service. A cybersecurity specialist quoted by TV 2 said this information could help criminals craft convincing scam messages impersonating a school.

perspectives.body: TV 2 reports that the exposed sender details and message openings may make impersonation scams more convincing, and says other organisations using external SMS services should check whether they are affected.

segments.title: Other organisations urged to check
segments.body: The Danish Agency for Societal Security says the provider’s services are used by multiple organisations and expects others may be affected. Schools have been advised to report the breach to the Data Protection Agency; students are urged not to click suspicious links or share personal information in unexpected messages.

content.headline: TV 2 says it will cooperate with police after being charged over documentary
content.shortHeadline: TV 2 charged over documentary, says it will cooperate with police
content.standfirst: Fyn Police have charged the broadcaster in connection with the 2024 documentary The Black Swan. Police have not publicly specified the charges; Berlingske has reported allegations of complicity in money laundering and handling confidential information, which TV 2 has not confirmed.

image.caption: TV 2’s headquarters in Copenhagen.

source.credit: Foto: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: TV 2 vil bistå politiet i opklaringsarbejde om Den sorte svane
TV 2 vil bistå politiet i opklaringsarbejde om Den sorte svane

segments.body: TV 2 has been charged in connection with its 2024 documentary The Black Swan, which used a hidden-camera source to expose alleged links between business figures, lawyers and the criminal underworld. Fyn Police confirm the case but have declined to say publicly what the charges are.

segments.title: Broadcaster’s response
segments.body: TV 2’s board chair says the station takes the charges seriously and will assist police. Its chief executive says she stands behind publishing the documentary and considers its findings sound. The station has not disclosed the specific allegations it faces.

perspectives.body: TV 2 says it will cooperate with the investigation while continuing to defend the decision to publish the documentary. The broadcaster has not confirmed the reported description of the charges.

segments.title: Questions about production
segments.body: Berlingske has reported that the charges concern alleged complicity in money laundering and the transfer of confidential information; police and TV 2 have not confirmed those details. Separate reporting cited by TV 2 says programme-makers were warned about legal risks before publication and that the production team supplied confidential case documents to a subject. TV 2 has apologised for the latter.

content.headline: Danish authorities recall Christmas biscuits over possible toxin risk
content.shortHeadline: Christmas biscuits recalled over possible toxin risk
content.standfirst: The Danish Veterinary and Food Administration says several kinds of biscuits may contain flour with elevated mycotoxin levels and advises people who have them to throw them away. The recall is linked to contaminated grain found at a Danish Agro storage site.

image.caption: Christmas biscuits are among the products recalled over a possible mycotoxin risk.

sources.originalTitle: Pebernødder, brunkager og vaniljekranse tilbagekaldes

segments.body: The Danish Veterinary and Food Administration has recalled several kinds of Christmas biscuits, including pebernødder, brunkager and vanilla wreaths, because they were made with flour that may contain elevated levels of mycotoxins. The agency says a health risk cannot be ruled out and advises consumers who have the products to discard them.

segments.title: Part of a wider recall
segments.body: The agency confirmed to Ritzau that the products are connected to the case of contaminated grain found at a Danish Agro storage site, where rat droppings were also reported. The products were sold by Lidl, Netto, Salling Group and Coop, among others. Some listed products may already be past their expiry dates.

segments.title: Earlier products also affected
segments.body: The biscuit recall follows recalls of other products made with ingredients linked to the grain case, including apple products, flour, pizza dough and bagels. The agency’s product list and expiry dates should be checked by anyone concerned about a specific item.

content.headline: Denmark to bar prosecutors from wearing religious head coverings in court
content.shortHeadline: Denmark to bar prosecutors from wearing religious head coverings in-c
content.standfirst: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked the director of public prosecutions to issue guidelines barring prosecutors from wearing religious head coverings in court. Prosecutor Zahra Sediqi says the rule could limit women’s professional opportunities; the government says it is about neutrality.

sources.originalTitle: Her er Zahra. Hun kan ikke længere være anklager i retten

segments.body: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked Denmark’s director of public prosecutions to introduce internal guidelines barring prosecutors from wearing religious head coverings in court. The rule would extend a restriction already set out in law for judges, but would be introduced for prosecutors through workplace guidelines.

segments.title: A prosecutor’s objection
segments.body: Zahra Sediqi, a prosecutor at the State Prosecutor’s Office in Viborg who wears a headscarf, says the rule could force her to remove it or take different duties. She argues that impartiality comes from professional conduct, not from whether a prosecutor wears a religious garment.

segments.title: Government’s case
segments.body: Wammen says prosecutors, like judges, should appear religiously and politically neutral in court. Sediqi disputes that the headscarf makes her less impartial and says the policy disproportionately affects women who wear it. The guidelines’ implementation and effect on her role remain to be seen.

content.headline: Danish pig farm cited after cats were seen eating from dead animals
content.shortHeadline: Danish pig farm cited after cats were seen eating dead pigs
content.standfirst: A veterinary inspection found six uncovered dead pigs outside a farm in Holbæk Municipality, with cats seen feeding on one carcass. The farm says it follows animal-handling rules; experts warn that exposed carcasses and contaminated feed could spread disease.

image.caption: A veterinary inspection video showed cats feeding on a dead pig at the farm.

sources.originalTitle: Flere overtrædelser: Styrelse fandt halvspiste svinekadavere uden for svinegigants stald

segments.body: The Danish Veterinary and Food Administration found six dead pigs outside a farm owned by Knud Kjær Knudsen during an inspection in August. An inspection video showed cats eating from one carcass, and the authority issued a formal warning requiring the farm to store dead animals under cover until collection.

segments.title: Possible health risks
segments.body: The inspection also found cat and bird droppings in feed grain and ordered it destroyed. A veterinary virology professor said parasites or other infection could, in some circumstances, pass from animals to pigs and potentially to people. The report describes possible pathways, not confirmed infections linked to the farm.

segments.title: Farm’s response
segments.body: Peter Kjær Knudsen told DR that dead pigs are moved to a loading area and then stored under a carcass cover or in a collection container. He did not address the finding of cat droppings in grain. The authority’s follow-up inspection in September found no problems with the checked storage of dead animals and slaughter waste.

content.headline: Jørn Hjorting, Danish radio host known for his warm voice, dies aged 95
content.shortHeadline: Jørn Hjorting, Danish radio’s warm voice, dies aged 95
content.standfirst: Hjorting presented De ringer – vi spiller for 28 years, inviting listeners to talk on air and choose a song. His family says he died after a short illness, leaving a legacy as one of Denmark’s best-known broadcasters.

image.caption: Jørn Hjorting at a press event in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: NEKROLOG Farvel til smilet, man kunne høre
Tidligere radio- og tv-vært Jørn Hjorting er død
Nekrolog: Jørn Hjorting var radioens og livets positive stemme

segments.body: Jørn Hjorting, one of Denmark’s best-known radio presenters, has died aged 95 after a short illness, his family and DR report. He hosted De ringer – vi spiller from 1968 to 1996, a programme in which callers chatted with him, answered a question and requested a song.

segments.title: A national audience
segments.body: Hjorting’s programme and Dansktoppen became major listener successes. The phone lines were so busy that the telephone company complained, and the show later used rotating final digits to spread calls around the country. His easy manner and interest in ordinary callers made him a familiar voice across generations.

segments.title: A deliberate optimism
segments.body: Hjorting also presented programmes including Morgennisserne and Giro 413 and held editorial roles at DR. He said he wanted his programmes to avoid dwelling on everything that had gone wrong and instead to be friendly and optimistic. His family says he leaves his wife Erna, children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

content.headline: Man charged over alleged sexual assaults during osteopathy treatments
content.shortHeadline: Man charged over alleged sexual assaults during treatments
content.standfirst: A therapist accused of presenting himself as an osteopath has been charged with sexual offences involving four female clients, including rape by a different sexual act, according to the indictment. He has not commented; the case is due in court in March.

sources.originalTitle: Falsk osteopat tiltalt for seksuelle krænkelser under behandlinger

segments.body: A therapist from Zealand has been charged with sexual offences involving four women who attended treatment sessions, according to an indictment obtained by TV 2. Prosecutors allege he touched clients inappropriately during treatment and that one incident amounted to rape by a different sexual act. The allegations have not been tested in court.

segments.title: Protected professional title
segments.body: The man is also charged with using the title osteopath without authorisation. Osteopath has been a protected title in Denmark since 2018. The Association of Danish Osteopaths says the man is not a member and that its members must be authorised or studying on an osteopathy programme.

segments.title: Case still to be heard
segments.body: The case is scheduled for two days in court in March 2027. The indictment indicates that the defendant denies the charges, although TV 2 says it has been unable to obtain comment from him or his defence lawyer. Prosecutors will also seek to bar him from providing massage or other physical treatment if he is convicted.

content.headline: Danish party proposes moving legal weddings from religious bodies to councils
content.shortHeadline: Enhedslisten proposes moving legal weddings to local councils
content.standfirst: Enhedslisten says legal authority to marry couples should belong to municipalities, with religious communities free to hold ceremonies. The Priests’ Association calls the proposal unnecessary and argues the current system accommodates religious freedom.

image.caption: Enhedslisten spokesperson Pelle Dragsted appeared on a Danish television programme.

sources.originalTitle: Enhedslisten vil ændre reglerne for kirkelige vielser – Præsteforeningen kalder det unødvendigt

segments.body: The Danish party Enhedslisten wants couples to marry at a municipality if they want a legally recognised marriage, leaving religious communities to conduct ceremonies without the legal function. The proposal follows comments by political spokesperson Pelle Dragsted and was elaborated by the party’s church spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach.

segments.title: A dispute over religious freedom
segments.body: Mach says the change would separate government responsibilities from religious ritual. Pernille Vigsø Bagge, chair of the Priests’ Association, calls the proposal unnecessary and says the existing system respects religious freedom. She argues that churches should retain the ability to conduct legally recognised marriages.

segments.title: Question of scope
segments.body: Enhedslisten points to cases in which church ministers refuse to marry same-sex couples as one reason to reconsider the arrangement. The party has not given a clear answer on whether it would also move authority over religious burials away from the church.

content.headline: Phoebe Bridgers’ phone-free arena show turns private grief into a shared release
content.shortHeadline: Phoebe Bridgers makes a phone-free arena feel intimate
content.standfirst: At Manchester’s Co-op Live, locked-away phones focused attention on a set shaped by grief and vulnerability. Two accounts find the restriction both inconvenient and unexpectedly freeing for the crowd and Bridgers alike.

image.caption: Phoebe Bridgers performs beneath the dome at Co-op Live in Manchester.

sources.originalTitle: Phoebe Bridgers review – phone-free arena show is a cosmic, communal revelation
Phoebe Bridgers’ controversial concert rule left me uneasy – but it was a revelation

segments.body: At a 23,000-capacity arena, the absence of glowing screens changes the feel of the room. The Guardian’s review describes Bridgers’ expansive, carefully staged show as a communal space where the crowd can attend to difficult songs rather than record them. Its emotional centre is “Still Standing”, her complex memorial to her father, met by audible sobbing.

segments.title: A different kind of attention
segments.body: The i’s reviewer also found the phone pouch frustrating before the show: it made checking a seat number and buying a drink harder, and raised concerns about communication in an emergency. Once the music began, though, the reviewer felt unusually absorbed—especially during “Still Standing”—and valued knowing the performance would not be turned into a stream of online clips.

perspectives.body: The i’s account gives the policy a practical counterpoint to the Guardian’s more atmospheric review: the inconvenience was real, but so was the relief of being present without checking or filming on a phone.

segments.title: The show behind the rule
segments.body: The Guardian describes the dome above the stage opening onto cosmic imagery, while Bridgers and her nine-piece band move from restrained arrangements to crashing crescendos. The crowd’s roar during “Motion Sickness” and the silence around her solo acoustic tribute suggest that the phone ban is not simply a restriction: it shapes the show’s movement between spectacle and closeness.

content.headline: Jennifer Reid carries the voices of Industrial Revolution workers into the world
content.shortHeadline: Jennifer Reid keeps working-class ballads alive
content.standfirst: The Manchester singer has learned hundreds of songs written by workers in Lancashire’s mills and mines. Her performances preserve their voices while drawing connections between industrial-era hardship and working conditions today.

image.caption: Jennifer Reid, who performs traditional workers’ songs from Lancashire.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’m like a lamp-post. Not glam, but vital’: Jennifer Reid, the singer saving the Industrial Revolution’s working-class songs

segments.body: Jennifer Reid began collecting and learning local broadside ballads while volunteering at Chetham’s Library. She now tours with a repertoire of about 300 songs, many in Lancashire dialect, and teaches children about the history and oral traditions around them. Her first gig was a performance at the 2013 Venice Biennale, after she persuaded artist Jeremy Deller to give her a place.

segments.title: Preserving the old shape
segments.body: Reid describes her approach as preserving the material before reshaping it. She studies archival recordings and dialect, and practised clog dancing to bring the rhythms of mill work into performance. The songs, she says, were written by workers themselves—not by people looking back on their lives from a distance.

segments.title: Then and now
segments.body: A trip to Bangladesh sharpened the contemporary resonance for Reid: she says garment workers’ songs there were strikingly similar to Lancashire ballads, and workers described conditions that recalled those of nineteenth-century factories. She stresses that the Industrial Revolution’s history must be understood alongside colonialism and suffering, not softened into nostalgia.

content.headline: Echobelly return with a new album after Britpop’s upheavals and years apart
content.shortHeadline: Echobelly find freedom in their return
content.standfirst: Sonya Madan and Glenn Johansson look back on Britpop’s excesses and describe making Eye-magi-nation, their first album in nearly a decade. The duo say self-releasing it after a label dispute gave them new creative freedom.

image.caption: Sonya Madan and Glenn Johansson of Echobelly in 2026.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We had a drug dealer called Satan on our tour bus’: Britpop stars Echobelly on debauchery, being pals with Oasis – and their spiritual return

segments.body: Echobelly’s Sonya Madan and Glenn Johansson recall a close friendship with Oasis and a turbulent US tour in 1994, including a visitor they remember introducing himself on their bus as “Satan”, a local drug dealer. Their new album, Eye-magi-nation, is due next spring and follows nearly a decade without a record.

segments.title: Making music on their own terms
segments.body: The pair, now Echobelly’s only official members, say a two-year dispute with their label led them to self-release the album. Madan describes the process as creatively freeing, though far from glamorous: she says she recorded vocals in the bathroom and wrote songs in a wardrobe to avoid disturbing the neighbours.

segments.title: A scene remembered differently
segments.body: Madan disputes the idea that Britpop’s male musicians were generally sexist, saying she found them kind, while describing rivalry and a lack of solidarity among some female-fronted bands. She also recalls the pressure of being pitted against other women by music journalists. Her account complicates, rather than settles, the debate over how women experienced the scene.

content.headline: Lizabett Russo returns to Transylvania for a searching, shape-shifting folk set
content.shortHeadline: Lizabett Russo makes a folk album of longing
content.standfirst: On Pe Unde Trece Dorul, the Scottish-based singer learns songs in remote Romanian villages and threads them into spectral, contemporary arrangements. The review praises her range and the album’s striking shifts in sound.

image.caption: Singer Lizabett Russo, whose album draws on Romanian folk traditions.

sources.originalTitle: The month’s best folk album: Lizabett Russo confronts her roots on an odyssey through Transylvania

segments.body: For her fifth album, Lizabett Russo returned to Romania, where she grew up, and travelled through Transylvania to learn traditional songs and calls. Its title, roughly translated as Where Longing Goes, comes from a song taught to her by farmer Maria Dulău, recognised as a Living Human Treasure by Romania’s National Institute of Heritage.

segments.title: Tradition in motion
segments.body: The review hears an album that moves between layered vocals, kaval, guitar and cello, with Russo’s voice shifting from gentle agility to an eerie a cappella delivery. Its centrepiece, “Dragă Mi-o Fost Lumea Mie”, builds from tender instrumentation into discordance, pauses for deep breaths, then returns to Russo’s voice.

segments.title: Other new folk records
segments.body: The review also recommends A Wild Inhabitation, a collaboration by Antoni O’Breskey and his daughter Consuelo Nerea Breschi; Claire Cronin’s spare, uncanny The Bruise; and Craven’s The Fruits of Idleness, Disgrace, and Death, which it calls a spirited collection.

content.headline: Morten Harket reflects on Parkinson’s, fame and a-ha’s early struggles
content.shortHeadline: Morten Harket on Parkinson’s and life beyond fame
content.standfirst: The a-ha frontman says his Parkinson’s diagnosis changed his access to singing and guitar, but also brought a new appreciation for the body. In a reader Q&A, he revisits early hardship, songwriting and the cost of sudden fame.

image.caption: a-ha frontman Morten Harket.

sources.originalTitle: a-ha’s Morten Harket: ‘My Parkinson’s diagnosis wasn’t devastating. I have a new appreciation for the human organism’

segments.body: Morten Harket says medication side-effects have affected his access to singing and guitar, and that the diagnosis forced him to reassemble his sense of self. He describes it not as devastating, but as a reason to appreciate the body’s complexity. For Human Grace, his new album, he and his collaborators drew on older recordings of his voice.

segments.title: The view from the early days
segments.body: Harket remembers a-ha’s first years in south London as exciting but precarious: the group lacked money and shared limited sleeping space in poor conditions. He says he never doubted the band would succeed, even when his bandmates were less certain, and recalls fame as a sudden, profound loss of ordinary life.

segments.title: A continuing search
segments.body: The answers range from memories of writing and faith to a reflection on what he thinks younger people seek: belonging and human connection. Harket says curiosity has remained central to him, even as he has become more sceptical about the world’s leaders and their willingness to take responsibility.

content.headline: Liz Harris lets the sounds of rivers flow through two film scores
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris finds music in water
content.standfirst: Music for Two Films About Water gathers Liz Harris’s scores for films by Tanja Engelberts and Takashi Makino. The review finds a lovely, if mostly instrumental, meeting of her ambient sensibility and the recordings of water themselves.

sources.originalTitle: Music for Two Films About Water

segments.body: Liz Harris, best known as Grouper, collects music for two short films on her first release under her own name. For Tanja Engelberts’ We Exhale, recordings of the Rhône River are woven into the composition, so the water’s changing volume helps map the spaces the film travels through.

segments.title: A quieter current
segments.body: The score for Takashi Makino’s Constellation is more static, mostly piano suspended in water sounds. The review says keeping the films’ recorded audio within the music connects with Harris’s history of working alongside experimental filmmakers, while noting that the album’s mostly instrumental textures give less room to the layered vocals that are among her strengths.

content.headline: Thoom turns hyperpop’s digital gloss into an expressive blend of Arabic sounds
content.shortHeadline: Thoom makes hyperpop intimate and ferocious
content.standfirst: On her debut, Los Angeles-based Zeynab Marwan combines hyperpop production with Arabic instrumentation and a forceful, shifting vocal style. The review finds the album most compelling when personal feeling and cultural identity meet.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: Zeynab Marwan, who records as Thoom, draws on hyperpop, Arabic instrumentation and the theatrical pull of Lebanese pop. Her debut, Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, was made with producers including Dylan Brady and Ike Clateman, and places her voice—by turns melodic, smoky and aggressive—at the front of the mix.

segments.title: Intensity with a sense of place
segments.body: The review highlights the pounding mizmar drone of “Janani”, the slow-burn warning in “Morocco” and the restless heartbreak of “Adfil”. Its final track, “I’m Going Back to Lebanon”, joins the pain of leaving a lover to uncertainty about returning home, asking whether the summer has ended and whether there is war again.

content.headline: Aphex Twin’s Drukqs still tests the boundaries between club music and concert-h,
content.shortHeadline: Aphex Twin’s Drukqs, 25 years on
content.standfirst: A new anniversary edition revives Richard D. James’s sprawling 2001 album, where breakbeats, prepared piano and electronic experimentation coexist. The review argues that its unruly scale is central to its achievement.

sources.originalTitle: Drukqs (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Twenty-five years after its release, Drukqs remains a 100-minute collision of Aphex Twin’s rhythmic ingenuity and a new interest in prepared piano. The review sees it as a bridge between electronic music’s club traditions and the more academic experiments of the concert hall, rather than a retreat from the dancefloor.

segments.title: Precision and excess
segments.body: On “54 Cymru Beats”, fast, intricate drums approach the point where rhythm blurs into pitch. Elsewhere, programmed Disklavier pieces turn an acoustic piano into something both mechanical and delicate. The album’s length and sharp shifts can be tiring, but the review argues that its apparent incoherence reflects music continually straining against boundaries.

content.headline: Mike Leigh says worsening myositis means Tender Loving Care will be his last
content.shortHeadline: Mike Leigh says his latest film will be his last
content.standfirst: After 55 years of filmmaking, the 83-year-old director says his worsening myositis has made the physical demands of directing impossible. He is not retiring, but regrets that he never made the big-budget contemporary film he wanted.

image.caption: Director Mike Leigh, whose latest film is expected to be his last.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Everybody tells me how I can keep working. My answer begins with ‘F’ and ends with ‘off’: Mike Leigh on 55 years of films – and why he’s just made his last

segments.body: Mike Leigh says Tender Loving Care, his 17th feature, is likely to be his last. His myositis has weakened his muscles and restricted his movement; he says directing has become physically beyond him, though he still intends to write. He had not realised during the film’s production that it would be his final one.

segments.title: A way of making films
segments.body: Leigh describes his long-established process as months of rehearsal and improvisation with actors, gradually distilled into precise scenes. He says he has never wanted a film to be a vehicle for a star, arguing that the expectation to cast big names can distract from the work and its collaborative development.

segments.title: The film he could not make
segments.body: Leigh says his lasting regret is that he could not secure backing for a large-scale contemporary story about friends from different ethnic and racial backgrounds, told across generations. A producer suggested developing it as television, but the BBC rejected the proposal. His latest film follows two social workers and the people around them, trying to care for one another in modern London.

content.headline: A Hollywood set builder turns cabin interiors into convincing in-flight scenes
content.shortHeadline: The specialist sets behind Hollywood’s airplane scenes
content.standfirst: Richard Chan’s Aero Mock-Ups supplies plane cabins, cockpits and details for films and television, from Bridesmaids to Focker-in-Law. The former pilot explains how an aviation salvage business became a niche part of Hollywood production.

image.caption: Aero Mock-Ups’ airplane-cabin set used in Focker-in-Law.

sources.originalTitle: Get me a 747 and deploy the oxygen masks! The British pilot behind Hollywood’s greatest inflight scenes

segments.body: When a film needs an airplane cabin, a cockpit or oxygen masks that really deploy, it may turn to Aero Mock-Ups, a Hollywood-based specialist run by British former pilot Richard Chan. Its work has appeared in films including Bridesmaids and Inception, as well as television series from Grey’s Anatomy to Westworld.

segments.title: From aircraft salvage to film sets
segments.body: Chan began collecting aircraft interiors and parts through his aviation work, initially intending to strip a Boeing cabin for salvage. A former secretary with experience as a script supervisor suggested showing it to production people; the cabin led to his first television job, and then to a business supplying detailed airline interiors and props.

segments.title: More than a film prop
segments.body: Aero Mock-Ups has also helped cabin crews and other teams practise safety procedures, and supplied a sensory room at San Francisco International Airport for travellers who are neurodivergent, anxious about flying or unfamiliar with air travel. Chan hopes to expand the warehouses into an airport set where a production can film from check-in through to boarding.

content.headline: You Can See Everything blurs the line between documentary and performance
content.shortHeadline: The reality games inside You Can See Everything
content.standfirst: The film’s staged intimacy with Elizabeth Holmes raises questions about truth, sympathy and the filmmaker’s role. One review sees a troublingly generous portrait; another traces its hall-of-mirrors approach to Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: Elizabeth Holmes is not the villain of You Can See Everything. That’s a problem
You Can See Everything overtly riffs on Vertigo. But how big is its debt to Kiarostami’s Close-Up?

segments.body: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes before she begins her prison sentence, with Fielder and a crew moving into her family’s life. The i’s review finds the result unsettling and engrossing, but says its domestic portrait leaves the viewer with a more sympathetic impression of Holmes than the reviewer expected.

segments.title: Who is directing whom?
segments.body: The Guardian connects the film’s mix of real people, reconstruction and performance to Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up, in which a man impersonates filmmaker Mohsen Makhmalbaf and Kiarostami inserts himself into the story. Co-director Oppenheim has named Close-Up as a favourite film. The comparison highlights how both works make it difficult to decide what is being staged and what is real.

perspectives.body: The i’s review focuses on the ethical risk of the film’s closeness: as Holmes is shown as a wife and mother, the documentary may invite sympathy while leaving the viewer unsure whether she is sincere or still managing the story.

segments.title: A question without an easy answer
segments.body: For The i, the uncertainty becomes particularly sharp after Holmes enters prison and Fielder’s attention shifts to her husband, Billy Evans. The reviewer argues that Evans’s behaviour threatens to displace Holmes as the subject of her own story, while leaving open the question of how much Holmes understands or participates in the film’s unfolding performance.

content.headline: Minotaur turns a Russian businessman’s corruption into wartime noir
content.shortHeadline: A Russian mini-oligarch in wartime noir
content.standfirst: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s first film in almost a decade follows a provincial businessman asked to supply workers for Russia’s war in Ukraine. The review finds a thriller about infidelity and violence whose political context sharpens its portrait of moral cowardice.

image.caption: A scene from Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur.

sources.originalTitle: Minotaur review – Andrey Zvyagintsev’s scorching noir intrigue amid the Ukraine war

segments.body: In Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, businessman Gleb is told that local firms must provide men for military call-up without disrupting the economy. He devises a scheme to recruit truck drivers on false promises of high pay, knowing they will be sent to war before he has to pay them.

segments.title: Power and evasion
segments.body: Gleb’s private crisis—he suspects his wife Galina is unfaithful—runs alongside the public machinery of the war. The review reads the film’s plot of infidelity and revenge through its larger portrait of disillusionment, political bad faith and the ways powerful people cover up their own misdeeds.

segments.title: Violence as a lesson
segments.body: When Gleb’s son says he is being bullied, his father advises him to threaten the boy who is tormenting him. The review sees this as a poisonous education in violence, but also a telling contrast with Gleb’s own cowardly, concealed schemes. Dmitriy Mazurov and Iris Lebedeva lead performances set against Zvyagintsev’s cold, crime-scene-like compositions.

content.headline: Avengers: Doomsday turns Marvel’s continuity into a puzzle for fans
content.shortHeadline: Marvel’s latest Avengers film comes with homework
content.standfirst: A new trailer appears to link Steve Rogers, the Fantastic Four and Doctor Doom through the MCU’s multiverse. The connections are still speculative, but the Guardian argues that piecing them together is part of the appeal for Marvel devotees.

image.caption: James Marsden as Cyclops in Avengers: Doomsday.

sources.originalTitle: Avengers: Doomsday has brought with it more ‘Marvel homework’ than ever. That’s just as it should be

segments.body: The latest Avengers: Doomsday trailer raises questions about the return of Chris Evans as Steve Rogers and the arrival of Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards at his home. The Guardian considers whether Rogers and Peggy Carter might have moved to another reality, and whether that could connect to the threat posed by Doctor Doom.

segments.title: Clues for the committed
segments.body: The speculation draws on earlier films and series: Rogers’ time travel in Avengers: Endgame, Loki’s role in holding the multiverse together, and the incursions described in Endgame: Encore. The article treats these connections as questions prompted by the trailer, not confirmed explanations, and argues that this kind of continuity-hunting is precisely what fans enjoy ahead of an Avengers release.

content.headline: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a laid-back macho fantasy
content.shortHeadline: Cliff Booth returns in a languid Hollywood caper
content.standfirst: David Fincher directs Brad Pitt in Quentin Tarantino’s spin-off about his Once Upon a Time in Hollywood stuntman. The BBC review enjoys its 1970s Los Angeles detail but finds little story, depth or respect for characters beyond straight white men.

sources.originalTitle: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review: Brad Pitt returns to his Oscar-winning role in a 'macho fantasy' ★★★☆☆

segments.body: Brad Pitt returns as Cliff Booth in a spin-off scripted by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher. Set in Los Angeles in 1977, the film follows Cliff as he spends time at a cinema, mixes margaritas and occasionally uses his wartime experience to scare off crooks threatening his film-industry friends.

segments.title: Atmosphere over momentum
segments.body: The review enjoys the film’s vintage cars, landline phones and old cinemas, and praises Elizabeth Debicki and Scott Caan in supporting roles. But Cliff’s encounters take a long time to lead to the central criminal problem, leaving the film, in the reviewer’s view, with a thin plot and a rambling, anecdotal shape.

segments.title: An old-fashioned point of view
segments.body: The BBC calls the film an antiquated macho fantasy, arguing that it gives little attention to anyone who is not a straight white man. Its conclusion is that the collaboration between two ambitious filmmakers delivers an easy-to-watch nostalgia piece rather than the daring work either might have made.

content.headline: Josephine asks how to show sexual violence through a child’s eyes
content.shortHeadline: Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child’s eyes
content.standfirst: Beth de Araújo’s film follows an eight-year-old who witnesses a rape, drawing on the director’s own experience. Its unflinching opening has prompted debate over the ethics and purpose of showing sexual violence on screen.

sources.originalTitle: 'The subject is still taboo': Shocking new film Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child's eyes

segments.body: Josephine begins when its eight-year-old title character comes across a rape in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. The film follows the trauma’s effects on her and her parents. Director Beth de Araújo says the story draws on her own experience of witnessing the aftermath of a rape when she was a child.

segments.title: A difficult choice
segments.body: De Araújo says she wanted viewers to encounter the event from a child’s perspective, before the child fully understands what rape is. The film took precautions around its young lead, Mason Reeves: a child psychologist was available to her family, she did not read the script, and she has not seen the finished film.

segments.title: What the scene is doing
segments.body: The article sets Josephine against earlier screen depictions of rape, some criticised for centring the perpetrator or using assault as spectacle. Film scholar Tanya Horeck says there is no single feminist rulebook for such scenes, but finds a case for this one because it shapes the child’s trauma and the rest of the film.

content.headline: Mark Gatiss’s The Bride’s Chamber may be his best Ghost Story for Christmas yet
content.shortHeadline: A Ghost Story for Christmas delivers a new high
content.standfirst: Martin Freeman plays a Dickens-like author drawn into a tale of cruelty and remorse in Mark Gatiss’s latest festive ghost story. The review praises its playful approach, dark subject and genuinely frightening supernatural finish.

image.caption: Martin Freeman as Francis Goodchild in A Ghost Story for Christmas: The Bride’s Chamber.

sources.originalTitle: A Ghost Story for Christmas: The Bride’s Chamber review – Mark Gatiss just made his best spooky festive tale yet

segments.body: The Bride’s Chamber adapts a Charles Dickens story from 1857, with Martin Freeman as Francis Goodchild, a writer who strongly resembles Dickens, and Jim Broadbent as the ghost who tells him of a cruel man and the young wife he urges to die. The Guardian calls the result tremendous fun, with a dark story at its centre.

segments.title: A tradition with room to roam
segments.body: The review places Gatiss’s revival alongside the 1970s Ghost Story for Christmas adaptations, but argues that his run has become a high point in its own right. Rather than return to the series’ familiar M R James stories, Gatiss has recently drawn on writers including Arthur Conan Doyle, E Nesbit and E F Benson.

segments.title: No easy redemption
segments.body: Unlike A Christmas Carol, this is not a story of reform or a happy ending: the review describes it as a tale of a bad man living with the consequences of what he has done. Its final supernatural flourish is praised as genuinely frightening, and as a mark of how the series can still surprise.

content.headline: Blade Runner 2099 makes a haunting television world of memory and decay
content.shortHeadline: Blade Runner 2099 is all neon and unease
content.standfirst: Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer lead the first television expansion of the Blade Runner story, where replicants hunt humans and memory has become contraband. The review praises its visual world while wishing for a firmer episodic shape.

image.caption: A scene from Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty

segments.body: Set 50 years after Blade Runner 2049, the series reverses the familiar hunt: blade runners are now replicants pursuing disobedient humans, while the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. Michelle Yeoh plays ageing blade runner Olwen; Hunter Schafer is Cora, a human passing as a replicant.

segments.title: A future built from images
segments.body: The Guardian says creator and writer Silka Luisa keeps the franchise’s future more atmospheric than neatly explained. The review revels in neon, shadows, abandoned spaces and a soundtrack of shimmering synths and soulful saxophone, describing a world where people try to cope as everything around them breaks down.

segments.title: An elliptical pursuit
segments.body: Olwen and Cora seek Olwen’s former colleague Marek, who appears to have gone rogue with a group of replicants. The review finds emotional force in their search for elusive memories, but says the series could have offered a stronger episodic structure without losing its strange, end-times mood.

content.headline: A new Pride and Prejudice joins TV’s long history of period drama
content.shortHeadline: The period dramas that still hold up
content.standfirst: As Dolly Alderton’s Netflix adaptation arrives, Guardian writers revisit the costume dramas that have endured—from Brideshead Revisited and Wolf Hall to The Crimson Petal and the White and Life on Mars.

image.caption: Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet and Jack Lowden as Mr Darcy in Pride and Prejudice.

sources.originalTitle: Tighten your corsets! Pass the smelling salts! It’s the greatest period dramas ever made

segments.body: Dolly Alderton’s new Pride and Prejudice, starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden, offers a reason to revisit television’s long relationship with period drama. The Guardian’s writers pick favourites across settings and styles, from the lavish locations of Brideshead Revisited to the pressured romantic stakes of Andrew Davies’s earlier Austen adaptation.

segments.title: More than costumes
segments.body: The selection makes the case for period drama beyond bonnets and stately homes: Wolf Hall is praised for translating Hilary Mantel’s novels into intimate, layered television, while Mad Men uses its recent past to examine the gradual unravelling of social conventions. Life on Mars turns nostalgia for the 1970s into a question about memory and reality.

segments.title: Lives beyond the drawing room
segments.body: Other choices take in the working lives and constraints beneath period spectacle, including The Crimson Petal and the White, about a sex worker navigating Victorian London, and a drama about the Brontë sisters’ struggle to publish and earn a living. The list also highlights queer history in Tipping the Velvet.

content.headline: Sweetpea’s second season finds its footing in a chaotic murder plot
content.shortHeadline: Sweetpea improves when it embraces the chaos
content.standfirst: Ella Purnell returns as Rhiannon, a meek journalist who murders men, in a season the Guardian still finds uneven. A copycat killer and a larger ensemble give the series more momentum, even as its feminist-revenge premise remains unsettled.

image.caption: Ella Purnell as Rhiannon in season two of Sweetpea.

sources.originalTitle: Sweetpea review – why was this disastrous serial killer comedy even given a second chance?

segments.body: Sweetpea returns with Rhiannon hiding a boyfriend’s body in her freezer and dealing with the guilt of having killed a blameless man in the previous season. The Guardian’s review recalls how the first run struggled to reconcile its everyday coming-of-age concerns with the violence of a vigilante-killer story.

segments.title: A wider cast, a messier story
segments.body: The new season adds a dynamic editor, a grieving mother and a doctor who treats Rhiannon’s recurring nosebleeds. When a copycat killer begins targeting men, the plot gains fresh momentum. The review says the show is more enjoyable when it stops pretending to be a coherent feminist-revenge story and leans into its eccentric, fast-moving chaos.

content.headline: Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List makes opting out its great pleasure
content.shortHeadline: Alan Carr’s comfort-first adventure show
content.standfirst: Carr tries activities with celebrity friends but does not have to finish anything he dislikes. The Guardian finds the lack of jeopardy—alongside his attempts at flying, bungee jumping and less intimidating outings—an unexpectedly soothing formula.

image.caption: Alan Carr and Mel Giedroyc in Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List.

sources.originalTitle: Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List review – the comfort show of my happiest dreams

segments.body: In Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List, the comedian attempts experiences with celebrity companions, including learning to fly a loop-the-loop with Mel Giedroyc and considering a bungee jump with Joanne McNally. The Guardian’s reviewer loves the premise that Carr can refuse any activity he does not want to complete.

segments.title: The appeal of no pressure
segments.body: Carr declines to take the controls of the plane and balks at other challenges, while still trying gentler pursuits such as driving a steam train, seeing a waterfall and going whale watching. The review argues that watching him opt out is more relaxing than the usual reality-TV tension of a celebrity being pushed past their limits.

segments.title: Company counts
segments.body: The programme’s pleasure also comes from Carr’s easy rapport with friends: the review highlights jokes about luxury-car airbags, an attempted interruption at a wedding and McNally’s own hesitation before a jump. Its verdict is uncomplicated: the half-hours are charming, funny and deliberately low-stakes.

content.headline: The Hunting Wives turns Texas culture-war politics into glossy soap
content.shortHeadline: The Hunting Wives plays both sides of Texas politics
content.standfirst: Netflix’s steamy drama returns to an affluent east Texas community of secrets and political divides. The BBC finds its satire of both liberal and conservative characters, and its focus on female pleasure, central to the show’s appeal.

sources.originalTitle: 'It appeals across demographics': How steamy soap The Hunting Wives took on sex, scandal and the US's blue-red divide

segments.body: The Hunting Wives follows Sophie, an East Coast political communications professional, and Margo, the wife of a Texas oil tycoon, as their affair develops amid a wealthy community’s secrets. The BBC says the show’s first season drew a large Netflix audience; the second, released on 26 November, brings more scandal and a murder investigation.

segments.title: Satire without a side
segments.body: The series makes fun of both the Republican elite and its Democrat-leaning newcomers. The BBC quotes TV critic Judy Berman, who argues that the characters’ focus on optics over ethics lets the drama satirise politics as performance rather than take a direct position on partisan issues.

perspectives.body: Texas Monthly editor Taylor Prewitt says the show’s cross-aisle teasing reflects the state’s varied politics, where people with opposing views often have to interact.

segments.title: The female gaze
segments.body: The BBC also highlights the series’ depiction of female pleasure, including scenes that are unusual for a mainstream glossy soap. Star Malin Åkerman says the show’s female creator, showrunner and directors helped shape its perspective on what women find sexy and beautiful.

content.headline: I’m a Celebrity’s “aggressive” label for AJ Odudu revives a familiar stereotype
content.shortHeadline: AJ Odudu and the “aggressive” label on I’m a Celebrity
content.standfirst: The i argues that journalist Mariella Frostrup’s description of presenter AJ Odudu on I’m a Celebrity reflects a recurring stereotype faced by Black women. Campmates disagreed with Frostrup, and producers reportedly spoke to her about the language.

image.caption: AJ Odudu on I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here!

sources.originalTitle: Mariella Frostrup’s behaviour is all too familiar to Black women like me

segments.body: After AJ Odudu questioned Mariella Frostrup’s claim to be pleased about help with cooking, Frostrup called Odudu “aggressive”. The i’s writer says the exchange looked different on screen: Odudu spoke softly, while Frostrup raised her voice, and the writer sees the label as part of a familiar pattern of Black women being treated as aggressive for reasonable behaviour.

segments.title: A disagreement in camp
segments.body: Wayne Rooney and Claire Sweeney, who saw the exchange, told Frostrup they did not think Odudu had been aggressive. The article says the two later attempted to clear the air, but Frostrup did not retract the word. Producers have reportedly spoken to her about her language; the piece notes that the impact on Odudu may outlast the argument itself.

content.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI makes routine and romance part of its criminal world
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI finds tenderness in the everyday
content.standfirst: The vast game can move from shootouts to grocery shopping, workouts and caring for a pet snake. The Guardian’s review finds new emotional weight in Jason and Lucia’s relationship, while a separate essay argues that routine is part of the game’s pleasure.

image.caption: Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple at the centre of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine

segments.body: The Guardian’s review describes Grand Theft Auto VI as an enormous, detailed world that accommodates both high-speed crime and ordinary activities, from shopping to assembling furniture. At its centre are Jason and Lucia, a fugitive couple whose attempts to build a life together give the game an emotional anchor.

segments.title: The pleasure of keeping things going
segments.body: A separate Guardian account focuses on Jason’s daily routine: getting dressed, working out, feeding his pet snake and handling errands. It argues that GTA VI makes tasks familiar from everyday life pleasurable through the game’s tactile world and the relationship between the characters.
