perspectives.body: The routine-focused piece argues that games often revolve around tidying, checklists and repeated tasks; GTA VI makes those rhythms appealing by connecting them to care for someone else.

segments.title: A different kind of GTA
segments.body: The main review sees the series’ familiar vulgarity and violent chaos alongside a new invitation to empathise. It says Lucia, the first female protagonist, changes how the game’s treatment of women lands, while noting the game remains deliberately offensive and has firmly earned its adult rating.

content.headline: Independent developers bring GTA-style chaos to their own cities
content.shortHeadline: Small studios make open-world crime games their own
content.standfirst: From a Manchester estate to 1970s Istanbul, independent developers are adapting the open-world template to places they know. Their games trade blockbuster scale for local detail, distinct settings and, in one case, a gentler take on crime.

image.caption: A scene from The Estate, set on a Manchester council estate.

sources.originalTitle: GTA in Istanbul? Meet the game developers bringing virtual crime chaos to their home cities

segments.body: The Guardian meets developers making open-world games in the spirit of Grand Theft Auto. Eamonn Swayah’s The Estate is set on a Manchester council estate, while Burak Akşahin’s Alaturka takes players to 1970s Istanbul. Both draw on places and cultural details rarely seen in blockbuster crime games.

segments.title: Local settings, different ambitions
segments.body: The Estate uses low-poly graphics, Mancunian radio chat and small-scale thefts to build its own sense of place. Akşahin’s game includes kebab-shop minigames and an Anatolian soundtrack, following a newcomer who hopes to earn enough to return to his village and marry.

segments.title: Beyond the copycat
segments.body: The article also describes Helsinki Online, a browser-based city sandbox whose creator has deliberately limited crime, and Last Drop, a darker Finnish game informed by stories of alcoholism. The developers see the influence of GTA as a starting point, not a requirement to reproduce its scale or approach.

content.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI’s soundtrack brings a star-studded new set of songs
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s album brings new music to Vice City
content.standfirst: Justice, Dua Lipa, Travis Scott and Latin artists feature on an album of new material tied to the game. The Guardian review sees the soundtrack as a showcase for Rockstar’s cultural reach and taste, with a few tracks that miss.

image.caption: Justice, who composed music for Grand Theft Auto VI and contributed to its soundtrack album.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album review – even GTA sceptics will warm to this zeitgeisty, star-packed soundtrack

segments.body: The soundtrack album for Grand Theft Auto VI collects new songs from artists including Justice, Dua Lipa, Travis Scott, Cardi B and Rauw Alejandro. Justice’s “Starting from Zero”, featuring Doobie Brothers singer Michael McDonald, opens with an ’80s-style pop ballad that nods to Vice City’s setting.

segments.title: A global radio dial
segments.body: The game itself contains 22 radio stations and 700 licensed songs across nine decades. The review highlights the breadth of the in-game music, from club-focused artists such as Arca and Rina Sawayama to the dreamy “Largate” by Helado Negro and Kali Uchis, while noting that the album is only a small part of what players will hear.

segments.title: A cultural platform
segments.body: The Guardian argues that Grand Theft Auto has become an unusually powerful music curator, with artists responding to the scale of the game and its audience. Not every selection works, the review says, but the record’s mix of pop, rap, rock and Latin music reflects a contemporary world beyond Vice City’s familiar 1980s nostalgia.

content.headline: Keepsake County turns suburban burglary into a bleakly funny survival game
content.shortHeadline: Keepsake County makes a life of stealing feel bleak
content.standfirst: This stealth game sends Samuel into oversized homes to steal whatever he can carry, from golf clubs to half-eaten pizza. The Guardian finds dark comedy in its break-ins and a melancholy story of debt and limited choices.

image.caption: A scene from Keepsake County.

sources.originalTitle: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience

segments.body: In Keepsake County, Samuel breaks into McMansions at dusk and steals whatever is within reach, often carrying his haul in a plastic shopping bag. The Guardian calls it a stealing simulator with eccentric, Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurd sense of humour, rather than a conventional crime drama.

segments.title: A lonely routine
segments.body: Players pick entry points, fiddle with locks and avoid residents, then sell the stolen goods at a pawn shop. As Samuel’s story emerges, the review reads his burglaries as a response to debt and medical bills he has little chance of paying. The game’s empty countryside loading screens add to its sense of isolation.

segments.title: Small-team limits
segments.body: The review praises the game’s economical story and its satire of suburban excess, but notes repeated dialogue and regions that do little to change the play. It also sees purpose in the repetition: Samuel’s situation is financially hopeless, and the routine of stealing becomes part of the game’s bleak point.

content.headline: A Zelda sceptic takes on Twilight Princess while GTA VI takes over
content.shortHeadline: A Zelda sceptic finds his way back to GTA
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s gaming columnist dusts off a Wii to try The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess, but struggles with its controls and dungeons. His eventual return to GTA VI becomes a funny reflection on belonging to gaming communities.

image.caption: The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess on Nintendo Wii.

sources.originalTitle: It’s the biggest ever month for video games – so why am I playing a title from 2006?

segments.body: With players celebrating a new Zelda remake and Grand Theft Auto VI dominating gaming conversation, the Guardian columnist tries to catch up by playing 2006’s Twilight Princess on a Nintendo Wii. The controls frustrate him, and he finds the game’s early tasks and dungeon puzzles hard to enjoy.

segments.title: Belonging has its limits
segments.body: The writer appreciates the game’s visuals and the transformation of Link into a wolf, but repeatedly loses his way in dungeons. He admits he kept going partly because he wanted to share in the enthusiasm around Zelda, before switching to GTA VI and finding a more familiar kind of play.

segments.title: Two communities
segments.body: The piece ends by arguing that games are also a way to connect with people we may never meet. The writer may not join the Zelda crowd, but sees the simultaneous excitement around two major releases as a rare moment for gaming’s different communities to share the spotlight.

content.headline: GTA VI’s seven scenic stops offer a break from crime and chaos
content.shortHeadline: Seven quieter places to explore in GTA VI
content.standfirst: From a mountain trail and a zoo to a remote lighthouse and an art museum, the Guardian picks places to explore in the game’s fictional Leonida when players need a break from its criminal missions.

image.caption: Mount Kalaga in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Seven beautiful places to visit in GTA VI, from mountains trails to an afternoon at the zoo

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto VI’s fictional Leonida offers more than missions and high-speed escapes. The Guardian’s guide points to places for slower exploration, including trails on Mount Kalaga, a Vice City zoo, a beach and a lighthouse reached by ferry or helicopter.

segments.title: A different pace
segments.body: The selection also includes a state park with dunes and seabirds, an art museum, a small island with a sculpture and a more upscale nightclub. The writer highlights the game’s scenery and oddities as destinations in their own right, rather than simply routes between story missions.

content.headline: NIH review links glyphosate to cancer, challenging EPA assessment
content.shortHeadline: NIH review challenges EPA’s glyphosate assessment
content.standfirst: A review of existing research by the US National Institutes of Health found an association with blood cancers in people and tumours in animals. The EPA has reached a different conclusion, and its reassessment is still under way.

image.caption: Roundup weedkiller containers on display in a San Francisco store.

sources.originalTitle: Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA

segments.body: The National Institutes of Health reviewed decades of research on glyphosate, a widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup. It found an association with blood cancers in humans and evidence that the chemical caused several types of tumours in animals. The NIH conducted a systematic review; it did not carry out new studies.

segments.title: A dispute over the evidence
segments.body: The findings conflict with the US Environmental Protection Agency’s recent conclusion that glyphosate is not carcinogenic. The EPA is conducting a court-ordered reassessment, expected early next year, after a court overturned its earlier assessment in 2022. The EPA did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

content.headline: Flu admissions in England rise as season starts earlier than usual
content.shortHeadline: Flu admissions rise as season starts early
content.standfirst: Hospital admissions in England rose sharply in the latest weekly figures, but an early start does not necessarily mean a more severe season. Scientists are weighing several possible reasons for the timing.

image.caption: Flu season began earlier this year, according to UK health officials.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are ill right now

segments.body: Flu admissions in England reached 9.0 per 100,000 people last week, up from 4.9 in the equivalent week last year. The UK Health Security Agency says this season began in October; officials described the latest rise in hospital demand as unusually early.

segments.title: What may explain the timing
segments.body: Possible explanations include changes in circulating flu strains, a later season in the southern hemisphere bringing more infections to the UK, and familiar winter factors such as cold, dry air and more indoor contact. These are possible contributors, not settled explanations. An early season does not by itself predict a worse one.

Flu often comes on quickly, with fever and muscle aches, unlike many colds, which more commonly bring a runny nose, sneezing and a sore throat. The UKHSA is urging people eligible for an NHS flu vaccine to get it; vaccination does not protect against the many viruses that cause colds.

content.headline: Blood tests could speed up Alzheimer’s diagnoses at more UK hospitals
content.shortHeadline: Blood tests may speed up Alzheimer’s diagnosis
content.standfirst: Some UK hospitals are beginning to offer a blood test in memory clinics ahead of the trials due to report in 2029. Wider access could shorten diagnosis, but availability remains uneven and private testing outside clinical care carries risks.

image.caption: A blood test could help doctors assess Alzheimer’s disease in people with memory problems.

sources.originalTitle: Blood tests that cut Alzheimer’s diagnosis from years to days coming in early 2027

segments.body: The test measures a form of tau protein called p-tau217, which can help doctors assess whether Alzheimer’s disease is likely. At present, diagnosis can take months or years and may involve brain scans and a lumbar puncture. University College Hospital in London is already offering the test, and Manchester Brain Health Centre says it will start soon.

segments.title: Access and limits
segments.body: Two large trials are examining how the tests could fit into NHS services and are due to finish in 2029. There is no central register of hospitals offering the test, and some people may otherwise have to pay privately. Doctors warn that testing outside a memory clinic could produce false positives; the test is used alongside clinical and cognitive assessment.

content.headline: New satellite method finds tides can vary by nearly a metre along a beach
content.shortHeadline: Satellite images reveal local differences in tide height
content.standfirst: Researchers used decades of satellite images to measure tidal variation along coastlines, finding differences of almost a metre across one New Zealand bay. The approach could help make local flood forecasts more precise.

image.caption: A New Zealand beach where researchers measured substantial variation in tidal height.

sources.originalTitle: How a new way of measuring tides could make flood forecasts more accurate

segments.body: Researchers from Technische Universität München and the University of Oxford used satellite photographs of shorelines as a measuring tool, analysing 40 years of images from Pacific coasts. They found that tidal height can vary substantially over short distances, including a difference of almost a metre across South Taranaki Bight in New Zealand.

segments.title: Why local measurements matter
segments.body: Tide gauges measure a specific point, while satellite radar measurements typically average across much wider areas. The researchers’ shoreline method could offer measurements at intervals of about 100 metres. More local detail could help identify which places are most vulnerable to storm surges, particularly where tide gauges are sparse.

content.headline: Lightning can injure people far from the strike: how to reduce the risk
content.shortHeadline: Lightning can injure people without a direct strike
content.standfirst: A couple struck by an electrical discharge at an Australian music festival recovered, but lightning can cause serious injuries indirectly. Experts explain how to assess storm risk and where to shelter.

image.caption: Lightning can cause fatal injuries directly or through electrical discharges nearby.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I felt a zap race through my body’: what happens when someone is hit by lightning?

segments.body: Caitlin Thomas and Harry Gordon were injured during a storm at a festival in Tocumwal, Australia. A lightning-risk expert believes they were affected by an upward electrical discharge near a metal-framed gazebo, rather than a direct strike. Electricity can also spread through the ground or jump from nearby objects, so a person need not be at the point where lightning hits.

segments.title: Finding shelter
segments.body: Experts advise going into a substantial building when thunder is heard; a hard-topped metal vehicle is the next-best option. Stay sheltered for 30 minutes after lightning stops. If shelter is impossible, keep your feet together, stay low and avoid lying down or sheltering next to a tree, where a side flash can reach you.

content.headline: Research finds memory scores have improved across generations
content.shortHeadline: Study finds better memory scores in later generations
content.standfirst: An analysis of more than 200,000 people found that those born later tended to score better on memory tests at the same age. The finding may help explain falling dementia risk for individuals, even as ageing populations increase total cases.

image.caption: An illustration accompanying research on memory and dementia risk.

sources.originalTitle: What to do at every age to stay sharp and stave off dementia

segments.body: The study analysed word-recall test results from more than 200,000 people born between 1910 and 1964. Participants born ten years later scored about 10% higher at age 60. The researchers say the pattern could help explain earlier findings of falling dementia rates by age, but it does not mean the total number of people living with dementia is falling.

segments.title: Possible influences
segments.body: The study cannot identify a single cause for the generational change. Researchers point to broad shifts in health and prosperity, while other work links factors such as education, smoking, cardiovascular health and hearing to dementia risk. The findings support the idea that risk can change, but do not establish which changes drove the memory scores.

content.headline: Reported breach of US Air Force cloud platform leaves key details unknown
content.shortHeadline: US Air Force cloud platform reportedly breached
content.standfirst: Reuters reports that hackers accessed Cloud One, a platform used for Air Force IT and logistics. The identity of the intruders, what they reached and whether data was taken have not been established publicly.

sources.originalTitle: Hackers reportedly breach US Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform

segments.body: The reported intrusion was discovered during a systems upgrade within the past month or so and caused disruption across the platform, Reuters reported, citing two sources. Reuters could not establish who was responsible, the extent of the intrusion or whether data had been stolen. The Air Force declined to comment on the security status of specific systems.

segments.title: Why Cloud One matters
segments.body: Cloud One supports Air Force functions including personnel information, pay, logistics and maintenance, and is used for systems that track munitions inventories. One source told Reuters that attackers exploited a software vulnerability to reach a control system; the source described what intruders could theoretically access, not confirmed activity.

content.headline: Google will require many Android app developers to publish contact details
content.shortHeadline: Google’s new rules put Android developers’ addresses at risk
content.standfirst: Developers classed as traders will have to publish a phone number and address from March, with Google saying the details will be visible worldwide. Apple, subject to the same EU rules, is limiting disclosure to relevant European countries and accepts PO boxes.

sources.originalTitle: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly

segments.body: Google says Android developers must declare by 1 February 2027 whether they count as traders under UK and European law. Those who do will have their contact details, including an address and phone number, displayed publicly from 1 March. Google’s definition broadly covers developers earning revenue from apps; hobby and non-commercial developers are exempt.

segments.title: Different approaches to compliance
segments.body: Google does not accept PO boxes for developer payment-profile addresses, leaving some independent developers to consider sharing a home address or paying for a business address. Apple is also subject to the regulations but says it will show addresses only in the relevant European countries and accepts PO boxes with supporting documentation. Google had not answered the Verge’s questions about its approach.

content.headline: Elevator mechanic shortage can delay repairs despite strong pay
content.shortHeadline: Why elevator repairs can take so long
content.standfirst: US mechanics can earn an average of $110,000, but employers say the trade is hard to staff and training takes years. Shortages can delay diagnosis, while some repairs also depend on parts that are difficult to source.

image.caption: Jim Lembesis, who has worked on elevators in Chicago for more than 47 years.

sources.originalTitle: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?

segments.body: Elevator technicians maintain and check the safety of systems that may be decades old. In the US, the average mechanic salary is $110,000, but the trade requires a four-year apprenticeship and some states require certification or licensing. Industry representatives say recruiting has become increasingly difficult.

segments.title: Skills and supply constraints
segments.body: A shortage can mean building managers wait days for a mechanic to diagnose a fault. But long repair delays are not always caused by a lack of staff: a replacement hydraulic cylinder can take six to 12 weeks to manufacture, according to the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. UK industry representatives also describe a worsening shortage and call for more investment in training.

content.headline: Tiny cars gain younger drivers as European sales double in five years
content.shortHeadline: Tiny cars find a new generation of drivers
content.standfirst: Sales of licence-free microcars across Europe have doubled over five years, with teenagers making up a growing share of buyers. Their low speeds and access rules offer mobility in some rural areas, but drivers and industry figures also raise safety concerns.

image.caption: Selena Buse uses her Citroën Ami to travel to school.

sources.originalTitle: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe

segments.body: European sales of tiny, often electric cars rose from about 30,000 to 60,000 in five years, according to the BBC report. In France, registrations increased from roughly 13,000 in 2019 to 25,000 last year. Depending on the country, young people can drive them from 14 to 16 after meeting local requirements.

segments.title: Mobility with limits
segments.body: The cars can offer independence where public transport is limited, and some teenagers choose them instead of scooters. Their maximum speed is 45km/h and they cannot use motorways or faster roads. One driver said the small vehicle felt less safe around larger traffic; sales in France have also flattened since subsidies for electric models were withdrawn.

content.headline: Amazon plans to launch its car-selling service in the UK in 2027
content.shortHeadline: Amazon plans UK car sales with Hyundai
content.standfirst: Amazon Autos is expected to launch in early 2027 with new Hyundai vehicles and used cars from Vertu Motors. Buyers will be able to browse and reserve online, but will complete purchases at dealerships.

image.caption: Amazon Autos, the retailer’s online vehicle-shopping service.

sources.originalTitle: Amazon to start selling cars in the UK next year

segments.body: Amazon says its UK service will initially offer new Hyundai electric, hybrid and petrol models, alongside used cars from British dealer Vertu Motors. Customers will be able to explore financing and reserve a vehicle online, then complete the purchase at a physical dealership. Amazon says it will announce more brands and dealers before launch.

segments.title: A new route into a large market
segments.body: The launch would take Amazon Autos beyond the US for the first time and put the retailer into a UK car market worth more than £200bn a year. Amazon presents the service as a simpler way to shop, while Autotrader points to the depth of its UK automotive data. The report does not establish how much the new service will change buyers’ existing dealership habits.

content.headline: Report warns AI could leave new police officers without core investigative
content.shortHeadline: Report warns AI could erode police skills
content.standfirst: A London Assembly report says relying on AI to sift evidence could leave inexperienced officers less able to judge when its answers are wrong. The Home Office says AI outputs must be checked by people.

image.caption: A report warns that over-reliance on AI could weaken police officers’ investigative skills.

sources.originalTitle: AI use risks eroding police skills, report warns

segments.body: Marina Ahmad, deputy chair of the London Assembly’s Police and Crime Committee, argues that officers develop judgement by doing work AI can now assist with, including reviewing evidence and learning patterns of offending. If new officers skip that work, the report warns, they may be less able to scrutinise AI outputs later.

segments.title: Oversight and rules
segments.body: Ahmad calls for training that keeps some investigative tasks in officers’ hands, as well as legislation and an independent regulator for police AI use. The Home Office says AI must be used lawfully and transparently, with human oversight and verification, and says government funding is intended to free up police time for frontline work.

content.headline: Retail workers say AI tools bring intrusive monitoring and faulty alerts
content.shortHeadline: Retail workers raise concerns about AI monitoring
content.standfirst: A Walmart cashier says inaccurate safety alerts interrupt her work, while unions warn that AI can intensify surveillance of staff and shoppers. Walmart says its tools are designed to support workers, not replace their judgement.

image.caption: A shopper in a Walmart store, where workers say AI tools can affect daily tasks.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s not helping’: calls for guardrails and regulations as AI use rises at US retailers

segments.body: A Walmart cashier in Oregon says an AI-linked safety system sends her repeated alerts, sometimes misidentifying shadows or stickers and requiring her to submit a photo before moving on in the app. She says the interruptions can keep her from helping customers. Walmart says its tools are people-led and that worker feedback helps improve them.

segments.title: A wider workplace concern
segments.body: Union representatives say AI can expand workplace surveillance, influence scheduling and discipline, and put pressure on workers through automated monitoring. They are calling for safeguards and a role for workers in decisions about how systems are used. A survey of retailers found AI already used or being introduced across areas including coding, cybersecurity, logistics and marketing.

Large-scale job losses attributed to AI have not yet materialised across retail, the report notes. But companies have announced planned cuts citing AI or technology investments, while workers and unions say the immediate effects include more monitoring and less room for human judgement.

content.headline: Cornwall Christmas market cancelled after backlash over AI-made images
content.shortHeadline: AI-generated market images prompt backlash and cancellation
content.standfirst: The Kernow Christmas Market was cancelled after visitors and traders objected that AI-generated promotional images misrepresented the event. A market industry chief says successful markets should reflect what customers will actually find.

image.caption: Totnes Market, cited as an example of a market rooted in its local community.

sources.originalTitle: Great markets 'reflect people who use them'

segments.body: The Kernow Christmas Market in Pool, Cornwall, was cancelled after a backlash over AI-generated promotional images that visitors and traders said did not match the event. Organisers said they would refund stallholders; one trader said he had spent months preparing stock and was left weighing an alternative venue.

segments.title: Why the images mattered
segments.body: David Catterall, chief executive of the National Association of British Market Authorities, says markets succeed when they represent their communities and accurately show what visitors can expect. The organisers said the market depended on an arrangement with Pool Market, which was responsible for practical elements including signage and decorating; Pool Market had not commented.

content.headline: Surrey County Council adopts rules for staff use of AI
content.shortHeadline: Surrey County Council sets rules for AI use
content.standfirst: The council’s new policy limits staff to authorised AI tools and bars uses that remove human oversight from decisions affecting residents. It also permits approved assistance with administration and data analysis.

image.caption: Surrey County Council’s policy allows some AI-assisted administrative work while requiring safeguards.

sources.originalTitle: Council adopts formal policy on AI use

segments.body: Surrey County Council has adopted its first formal AI policy. Staff may use AI for approved tasks such as administrative assistance and data analysis, but cannot use internet-accessed tools such as Gemini or ChatGPT for council work over data-security concerns. The policy says any AI use must be safe, ethical, lawful and appropriate.

segments.title: Safeguards and consequences
segments.body: The policy prohibits removing human oversight from decisions affecting residents, unfair discrimination and generating misleading information. Breaches of data-protection, confidentiality or security rules are also prohibited and can lead to disciplinary or contractual consequences. Councillor David Lewis said safeguards should not be so restrictive that they obstruct responsible use.

content.headline: Agriculture students say hands-on skills still matter as AI enters farming
content.shortHeadline: Agriculture students weigh AI against hands-on skills
content.standfirst: Colleges in East Yorkshire and Lincolnshire report rising enrolment in some land-based courses, as students learn how AI can support farming while stressing the work people still do themselves.

image.caption: A Bishop Burton College student says AI cannot replace practical livestock skills.

sources.originalTitle: AI is great, but it can't deliver a lamb, say students

segments.body: Students at Bishop Burton and Riseholme colleges are learning about AI in agriculture alongside practical skills. They say the technology can help farmers gather information and spot problems, but cannot carry out tasks such as handling livestock or repairing equipment in a field.

segments.title: What the survey suggests
segments.body: Bishop Burton College said 46% of 2,000 secondary-school pupils it surveyed had considered a more hands-on career because of AI. It also said 77% of 2,000 parents were concerned about AI’s effect on their children’s job prospects. These are survey findings from the college, not evidence that AI is driving the reported rise in course enrolments.

content.headline: Australia’s sandpapergate inquiry expands to include the 2017-18 Ashes
content.shortHeadline: Australia’s ball-tampering inquiry widens to include 2017-18 Ashes
content.standfirst: Cricket Australia’s independent forum will examine ball-management practices across the 2017-18 season, including the Ashes and the tour of South Africa that brought the scandal to light. It will not impose retrospective sanctions.

image.caption: Australia won the 2017-18 Ashes series against England 4-0.

sources.originalTitle: Australia's sandpapergate probe to also include 2017-18 Ashes

segments.body: Cricket Australia has widened its independent inquiry into the ball-tampering scandal to include the 2017-18 Ashes, which Australia won 4-0. Its remit covers ball-management practices across the men’s team that season, all four Tests on the subsequent South Africa tour and the investigation that followed.

segments.title: Disputed accounts
segments.body: The inquiry follows renewed scrutiny after former batter Usman Khawaja said in his autobiography that the team knew about the plan to tamper with the ball in the third Test in Cape Town. Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Pat Cummins have denied knowledge; Cummins called Khawaja’s account “nonsense”. David Warner and Cameron Bancroft have backed Khawaja’s version.

Everyone involved in the 2018 tour, including players and support staff, will be invited to give evidence, but participation is voluntary and information will be confidential unless a participant says otherwise. Cricket Australia says the forum will run for six weeks and it will publish the report and recommendations within 30 days of receiving them. No retrospective sanctions will be imposed.

content.headline: Ten-man Bournemouth make it five European wins in a row
content.shortHeadline: Ten-man Bournemouth extend record run to 10 wins
content.standfirst: Bournemouth came from behind at Celta Vigo after Bafodé Diakité’s first-half dismissal, winning their fifth European match in a row. The result also made it 10 consecutive wins in all competitions, a club record.

image.caption: Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose, who took over in the summer.

sources.originalTitle: Bournemouth 'allowed to dream' as fans book Europa League final hotels

segments.body: Bournemouth trailed to Iago Aspas’ goal and were reduced to 10 men when Bafodé Diakité was sent off midway through the first half. They still won at Celta Vigo, with second-half goals from Álvaro Rodríguez and Rayan completing the comeback. The Cherries have now won 10 matches in a row in all competitions, a club record.

segments.title: A European run to dream on
segments.body: Bournemouth are the only team to have won all five of their Europa League matches so far and sit top of the table. They are closing in on a top-eight finish, which would take them straight to the last 16 without a play-off. Alex Scott called winning the competition the team’s dream, while head coach Marco Rose said there were still many games to go.

content.headline: No post-match drug tests during South Africa-New Zealand rugby series
content.shortHeadline: No post-match drug tests during Springboks-All Blacks series
content.standfirst: Anti-doping authorities conducted no post-match tests during the four-Test series, despite such testing being standard at many elite fixtures. World Rugby pointed to its year-round testing programme but did not confirm the reported absence of tests.

image.caption: The Springboks and All Blacks played three Tests in South Africa and a fourth in Baltimore.

sources.originalTitle: No post-match drug testing in South Africa v New Zealand series

segments.body: South Africa and New Zealand players were not given a single post-match drugs test during their four-Test series in August and September, BBC Sport reports. The matches took place in South Africa apart from the final Test in Baltimore. The series agreement referred to World Rugby’s anti-doping rules, but post-match testing was not carried out.

segments.title: The wider testing picture
segments.body: World Rugby did not confirm the absence of tests in the series. It said its risk-based, no-notice programme tests players throughout the year, including during international windows; South Africa’s anti-doping body referred questions back to World Rugby. The report also notes that South Africa’s testing body recorded 225 rugby tests in its latest annual report, down from 753 a decade earlier, and says overseas laboratory costs have risen.

content.headline: Germany forward Laura Freigang banned for 16 months over testing failures
content.shortHeadline: Freigang banned for 16 months after three testing failures
content.standfirst: Germany and Eintracht Frankfurt forward Laura Freigang has been suspended over three reporting and/or testing failures. The ban rules her out of next summer’s Women’s World Cup and sidelines her from football activity until after 7 October 2027.

image.caption: Germany forward Laura Freigang has scored 17 goals in 45 appearances for her country.

sources.originalTitle: Germany's Freigang banned over drugs test issues

segments.body: Laura Freigang has been suspended for 16 months after a dispute-resolution agreement with the German Football Association, the World Anti-Doping Agency and Germany’s National Anti-Doping Agency. The case concerns three reporting and/or testing failures between 11 March 2025 and 23 February 2026. She can return to training two months before the ban ends, but cannot play until after 7 October 2027.

segments.title: Impact on club and country
segments.body: The suspension means Freigang will miss next summer’s Women’s World Cup. Her personal records for appearances, goals, assists and other statistics from 23 February 2026 have been nullified, although Eintracht Frankfurt’s results are unaffected. She has scored six goals and made two assists in 11 league starts this season. The club says it will discuss the terms of her future employment with her.

content.headline: Great Britain beat Germany to reach Davis Cup semi-finals
content.shortHeadline: Patten and Skupski seal Great Britain’s Davis Cup semi-final place
content.standfirst: Henry Patten and Neal Skupski won the deciding doubles match to send Great Britain past third seeds Germany in Bologna. The team reaches the last four for the first time since 2019 and will face Spain on Saturday.

image.caption: Henry Patten and Neal Skupski celebrate their doubles win over Germany.

sources.originalTitle: GB win decider to reach Davis Cup semi-finals

segments.body: Cameron Norrie put Great Britain ahead with a three-set win over Jan-Lennard Struff, before Alexander Zverev beat Arthur Fery to take the tie to a deciding doubles match. Patten and Skupski then defeated Kevin Krawietz and Tim Pütz 6-2 7-6 (8-6), saving five break points in the first set and recovering from a mini-break down in the tie-break.

segments.title: A first semi-final since 2019
segments.body: The win puts Great Britain in the Davis Cup semi-finals for the first time since 2019. Patten and Skupski, who are set to partner up for the 2027 season, have won all three of their Davis Cup matches together. They are scheduled to face Spain on Saturday; Spain’s singles wins meant Carlos Alcaraz did not need to play in the quarter-final, though captain David Ferrer said he could be in contention for the semi-final.

content.headline: Camilo Duran’s late winner keeps Celtic’s Europa League hopes alive
content.shortHeadline: Duran strikes late to keep Celtic’s European campaign alive
content.standfirst: Camilo Duran came off the bench to head Celtic past Portuguese second-tier side Torreense, continuing a prolific season and keeping the club within reach of a Europa League play-off place. The performance also renewed questions about the team’s wider struggles.

image.caption: Camilo Duran has scored 15 goals this season for a Celtic side pursuing European progress.

sources.originalTitle: 'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?

segments.body: Celtic were labouring against Torreense until Camilo Duran came on with just over half an hour remaining and scored a late winner. The 24-year-old has now scored 15 goals and provided six assists in 23 appearances this season. Manager Martin O’Neill called him “priceless” and said he had taken on the role of “the man”.

segments.title: More than one player’s burden
segments.body: Duran’s goals have helped keep Celtic within reach of a Europa League play-off place with three fixtures remaining, and have also proved decisive in domestic matches. But the report describes a side short of attacking ideas against Torreense, with limited contributions from several players and no driving force in midfield. Celtic remain only a point clear of Rangers, and the account argues that Duran may need to sustain his form if the club are to progress.

content.headline: Former England scrum-half and rugby commentator Nigel Starmer-Smith dies at 81
content.shortHeadline: Nigel Starmer-Smith, former England player and commentator, dies at 81
content.standfirst: Starmer-Smith made seven appearances for England before a long career in broadcasting, including 15 years voicing the BBC’s Rugby Special. His son said he died peacefully after a long battle with dementia.

image.caption: Nigel Starmer-Smith voiced the BBC’s rugby highlights programme Rugby Special for 15 years.

sources.originalTitle: Former England scrum-half Starmer-Smith dies aged 81

segments.body: Nigel Starmer-Smith, former England scrum-half and rugby union commentator, has died aged 81. He represented Harlequins and the Barbarians and played seven times for England between 1969 and 1971. After retiring in 1976, he became a broadcaster and journalist, voicing the BBC’s Rugby Special for 15 years and commentating for ITV at the 2003 Rugby World Cup.

segments.title: Remembered by his family
segments.body: Starmer-Smith had been diagnosed with dementia in 2015. His son Charlie said he died peacefully after a long battle with the condition, which he said had robbed his father of his ability to communicate. He remembered him as a rugby player, commentator, writer, fundraiser and family man, and asked those who knew him to remember a happy moment and smile.

content.headline: Selby starts UK Championship defence against Matt Selt
content.shortHeadline: Selby draws Selt as UK Championship begins on Saturday
content.standfirst: Mark Selby opens his title defence against Matt Selt at the UK Championship in York. Ronnie O’Sullivan faces Jack Lisowski, while Mark Allen is set to return to the tournament after a five-month break from the sport.

image.caption: Mark Selby is defending his UK Championship title in York.

sources.originalTitle: Selby faces tough UK opener while Allen set to feature

segments.body: Four-time world champion Mark Selby begins his UK Championship title defence against Matt Selt on Saturday. Selt reached the televised stages by beating Jak Jones, the highest-ranked player in qualifying. The tournament, the season’s first Triple Crown event, runs from 28 November to 6 December at York Barbican, with a top prize of £312,500.

segments.title: A notable return and a marquee tie
segments.body: Ronnie O’Sullivan has been drawn against Jack Lisowski, who set up the match with a 6-4 qualifying win over Mark Joyce. Mark Allen is set to face Yuan Sijun after returning to the sport following five months away; he lost to Jordan Brown in his first-round match at the Northern Ireland Open in October. Allen spoke publicly about mental health struggles last month.
